$comment: A Burj-class reference building — GitHub issue #376, DECISIONS.md § D527, docs/38 § 2.5. 165 levels, 57 lifts, 8 escalators, speeds to 10 m/s. THE ARITHMETIC, so nobody re-derives it: two basements (B2, B1) plus G and floors 1–162 is 165 levels, of which 163 are at or above ground. Floors 154–162 are mechanical and carry no population; 2–153 are populated, which is 152 floors, and the reference's 'about 154 populated floors' is honoured as a shape rather than transcribed floor by floor — the six sky-lobby levels (43/44, 76/77, 123/124) are transfer floors and carry no residents either. POPULATION AND MIX ARE AN ASSUMPTION, NOT A CITATION, which § D527 leaves to this file: the per-floor figures fall from 29 in the lower office zone to 12 in the upper residential one, summing to 3198, and no published occupancy for the reference tower was available to the author. THE FIGURE IS MEASURED RATHER THAN GUESSED: it is what this 57-lift arrangement serves at `office-standard` with a valid AWT. Measured over a 1 800 s window, seed 376, `collective`: 3 198 people give a 35 s mean wait, a 98 s 95th percentile and nothing undelivered; 5 307 saturate (175 s, AWT suppressed) and 10 614 leave 422 of 4 457 journeys unserved at a 791 s mean. So a published occupancy higher than this does not merely change a field — it says the reference tower's real lift count is not 57 on this arrangement, which is the kind of thing this building exists to expose. Declared as an assumption so a later citation replaces a stated one rather than a silent one. OCCUPANCY, CHECKED AND NOT ADMITTED — GitHub issue #438, approved by the owner on 2026-09-10. The sentence above saying no published occupancy was available was true when it was written and is kept; what changed is that two published figures were found on 2026-09-10, and neither is an occupancy this file can use. 35,000 is published by Arcadis, which lists itself as the tower's architect and engineer of record, as the workers and residents the tower would accommodate, and by Al-Kodmany, Buildings 2015, 5(3), doi:10.3390/buildings5031070, § 3.3.1, as what the tower can hold. Neither states a basis and neither says daily; the daily wording that prompted #438 comes from a 2026 trade article whose only link carries no such figure. It is rejected as a resident-plus-worker count on arithmetic rather than taste: Emaar's own fact sheet gives 900 homes, 144 Armani residences and over 300,000 sq ft of office, and at a generous four people a home and two a room over CTBUH's 304 hotel rooms, the office would have to hold about 30,200 people in about 27,900 m², under 1 m² each. What 35,000 does count is not established, and no mechanism is offered here. 12,000 residents and workers appears once, in Gulf News on 2010-02-01, with no source, and is not a citation. BOTH SIT ABOVE THIS FILE'S OWN BRACKETS — 5 307 saturate and 10 614 leave 422 of 4 457 journeys unserved — so if either is ever confirmed as a resident-plus-worker population, the measurement above already says 57 lifts on this arrangement do not serve it at `office-standard`, and a run at that figure would say by how much. Rejecting 35,000 does not place the real figure below 5 307 either. The figure stays 3198, and it stays an assumption. The traffic profile is office-standard because the lower half is offices and the profile library ships nothing mixed-use with a supertall's shape; that too is an assumption. The reference is a floor, not a ceiling (§ D527). DECK LOAD, CHECKED AND NOT ADMITTED — GitHub issue #438, approved by the owner on 2026-09-10. Three published per-deck figures exist and they disagree about the same two cars: 23 persons a deck in Otis's 2005 contract announcement as FMLink reported it; 12 to 14 people per cab in the completion coverage quoting Emaar (Dubai Chronicle, 2009-12-30) and in Al-Kodmany 2015; and 21 persons a deck in Gulf News and on a Prysmian page, neither citing a source. No rated load in kilograms was found from Otis, Emaar or CTBUH. Every one of them describes the tower's two double-deck OBSERVATION cars, not a sky-lobby shuttle, so none is a figure for the `shuttle` bank. MEASURED AGAINST THE CATALOGUE: 21 a deck is a 6 300 lb car by this file's ratedLoadLb / 150 and a 7 055 lb car at EN 81-20 Table 6's 1 600 kg row, 1.26x and 1.41x the `ultra-high-speed` ceiling of 5 000 lb, and 21 is also outside that class's 12-14 persons a deck. That is two warnings, `load-outside-class-range` and `deck-persons-outside-class-range`, not one. The shuttle stays at 2 000 lb a deck: 13 persons at 150 lb and 12 at 75 kg, inside both ranges and inside Emaar's 12 to 14. THE 504 m RECORD, CHECKED — GitHub issue #438, approved by the owner on 2026-09-10. 504 m is a published record (Guinness World Records, 2014; Emaar's fact sheet; Al-Kodmany 2015), and the operator gives it to a SERVICE lift: Emaar's fact sheet lists it as the tallest service elevator, and the completion coverage quoting Emaar gives the main service elevator that rise, at 9 m/s (Dubai Chronicle, 2009-12-30). Otis's 2005 announcement and the Skyscraper Museum's pre-completion page gave the longest travel to the observation cars instead; as built, the observation deck is at 452 m (Emaar), so no post-completion source shows a passenger car running 504 m. That moves nothing here: `observation` serves only G, 1, 123 and 124, so a trip from the lobby to 124 is a single run of up to 496.0 m, and `shuttle` spans the same rise — 44 m more than the real observation run, because every floor in this file is 4.0 m. The car the record belongs to is a service lift, and this file has none, for the measured reason in its notes. 57 LIFTS AND 60 SECONDS, CHECKED — GitHub issue #438, approved by the owner on 2026-09-10. 57 elevators and 8 escalators is Otis's own count (press release, 2024-03-06) and the count in the 2009 completion coverage quoting Emaar; CTBUH's Skyscraper Center counts 58 cars including freight. The 57 counts lifts only, and it includes lifts that are not passenger cars — the completion coverage names a main service elevator and a spire service lift, and Al-Kodmany 2015 names 5 500 kg service elevators and a circular restaurant lift — so this file's 57 passenger cars are more than the tower's passenger fleet, and 5 307 is optimistic rather than conservative. Otis gives the tower two double-deck cars, both observation, running ground to levels 124 and 125 in 60 s at up to 10 m/s; that agrees with the 10.0 m/s `observation` bank, apart from its 44 m of extra rise. No source found shows the sky lobbies served by double-deck cars, so the note calling the 14-car double-deck shuttle the arrangement the reference tower uses is unsourced.

transportModes.$comment: The escalator at the ground lobby, joining the two boarding decks a double-deck shuttle serves. Traversal time is DERIVED, not quoted, by `vertical-city.json`'s own method so the two files cannot disagree: rise 4.0 m; inclination 30 degrees, which BS EN 115-1 makes the only permitted angle above a 6 m rise and which is the common commercial compromise below it; nominal speed 0.5 m/s (EN 115-1 permits up to 0.75 m/s at 30 degrees). Incline length = 4.0 / sin 30 = 8.00 m, so 16.0 s on the incline; EN 115-1's two flat steps at each landing at 0.40 m step depth add 1.60 m of horizontal run, or 3.2 s. Total landing to landing 19.2 s. No CIBSE Guide D lumped escalator traversal figure was available to check this against; see docs/02-elevator-reference.md. MEASURED, and say which count this is: routing all 27,060 ordered floor pairs through RoutePlanner/routeTopologyOf, this edge lies on the shortest route for 6 of them (6, 8, 8 and 6 across the four, 28 in all) -- pinned in packages/viz/src/record/burjReference.test.ts and published in docs/04-test-buildings.md § 9. This is a count over the TOPOLOGY, every pair weighted once. It is NOT the quantity vertical-city's modes record: traffic/transportRoute.test.ts#HOPS_BY_MODE counts hops taken by the 1,956 passengers of a generated day, so its 266 and its two zeros are demand-weighted and this number is not comparable with them. The dead-field question data/buildings/README.md's rule exists for -- does anybody actually use this machine? -- is the demand-weighted one, and for this building it is UNMEASURED.

notes: 57 lifts in six banks: one double-deck sky-lobby shuttle of 14 cars serving G/1 and all three sky-lobby pairs, four local banks (10, 10, 11 and 8) and four observation expresses. 14+10+10+11+8+4 = 57.

THERE ARE NO SERVICE LIFTS, and that is a finding about the model rather than a simplification. Five were declared at first, reaching every level as a real building's do. Two measurements refused them. **One**: while they served the passenger lobby they were the only banks spanning the entrance to the top, so the dispatcher never had to transfer anybody — the fourteen shuttle cars carried ZERO legs and `service-high`'s two carried 277 of 827 at a 624 s mean wait, with 1.03 legs a journey against `vertical-city`'s 1.65. **Two**: moved to the loading dock they still overlapped every local, and `config/buildingConnectivity.test.ts` requires every floor served by more than one bank to be declared a transfer floor — which would have made 148 of 165 floors transfer floors and emptied the concept. This model has no notion of a staff-only bank; `accessZones` gates floors, not banks. So the honest shape is a building without them, recorded here, rather than 148 floors mislabelled. The plant floors 154–162 are reached by `local-zone3`, so every level is still routable.
The three sky lobbies are at 43, 76 and 123, each a two-level transfer served by a double-deck shuttle — the arrangement the reference tower uses and the one § D131's paired stops model.

Escalators are eight, in four pairs, each joining the two boarding decks of a double-deck level. #376's fourth criterion measures their hop count before any capacity or direction is added: as modelled they are undirected and uncapacitated, and data/buildings/README.md's rule is that a declared mode with zero hops is a dead field.

FOUR ESCALATORS ARE DECLARED AND THE REFERENCE TOWER HAS EIGHT, which is #376's fourth criterion answered by measurement rather than by transcription. All 27 060 ordered floor pairs were routed: every one is reachable, 24 routes use an escalator, and with eight declared — a pair at each double-deck landing — **four of them took zero hops**. As modelled an escalator is an undirected, uncapacitated edge with a traversal time, so the second of an identical pair can never be chosen: the router takes one and the other is a dead field, which `data/buildings/README.md` forbids. So one edge per landing is declared, and the finding is recorded here rather than papered over. THIS IS THE MEASUREMENT § D527 ASKED FOR BEFORE ADDING CAPACITY OR DIRECTION: a second escalator can only change a decision once an escalator can be full or one-way, and until then declaring eight would be declaring four lies.
